Case Vignette: "Sergeant First Class L."

Sergeant First Class L. is a 20-year-old married woman of South Eastern Asian descent who presents as a quiet, composed young woman with a military bearing that seems to sit uneasily on her, like a uniform that no longer fits. She is a soldier in an active-duty infantry unit, a role she chose at eighteen to escape a family that, in her words, "expected me to be a good daughter, not a good fighter." She married her husband, a fellow soldier, six months ago, and they live on base.

The event that brought her to my office happened eight months ago, during a routine field exercise. She was on a night patrol with her squad, a standard security sweep through a training area that was supposed to be empty. She had been walking point, a position she had earned through hard work, when a soldier from another unit-a man she had never met-stepped out of the shadows of a supply tent. He was drunk, she later learned. He grabbed her by the arm, pulled her behind the tent, and assaulted her. It was not a combat wound. It was not an enemy. It was a fellow soldier, a man who wore the same uniform she did.

In the immediate aftermath, she did not scream. She did not report it. She told herself it was a mistake, a misunderstanding, that she had overreacted. She finished her shift, walked back to her barracks, and took a shower so hot it left her skin red and raw. She scrubbed her arms with a brush until they bled, trying to erase the feeling of his hands. She told no one. Not her squad leader. Not her husband. She told herself that she was a soldier, and soldiers do not break.

The weeks that followed were a slow, grinding erosion of her normal life. She began to avoid the motor pool where the supply tent had been, taking long detours even if it made her late. She stopped going to the mess hall at night, preferring to eat alone in her room. She stopped sleeping in the same bed as her husband, claiming she was "too hot" or "too tired." In truth, the feeling of another body next to her, even his, made her chest tighten and her throat close. She began to wake up at 2:47 AM every single night, the exact time she remembered the assault ending, drenched in sweat, her heart pounding so hard she could hear it in her ears. She would lie there, rigid, replaying the moment-the smell of cheap whiskey, the sound of his breathing, the weight of his hand over her mouth.

Her husband noticed. He asked if she was okay. She said she was fine. He asked if she was angry with him. She said no. He asked if she wanted to talk. She said nothing. The silence between them grew heavy, like a third person in the room.

Her work began to suffer. She was a sharp soldier, known for her quick thinking and steady aim. Now, she flinched at sudden noises-the slam of a vehicle door, the crack of a branch underfoot. During a live-fire exercise last month, she froze. She was supposed to engage a target, but she saw a figure in the corner of her eye, a shape that looked too much like the man in the shadows. She could not pull the trigger. Her squad leader pulled her aside and asked if she was "losing her nerve." She said no, but she knew it was a lie.

She is here today because her husband finally found her, sitting on the bathroom floor at 3:00 AM, crying silently, her uniform still on. He did not yell. He just sat down next to her and said, "I don't know what happened, but I'm not leaving." She told him the next morning. He held her hand and drove her to the clinic.

In session, she sits very still, her hands folded in her lap. She speaks in short, clipped sentences, as if she is giving a report. She tells me she feels "numb" most of the time, like she is watching her life from a distance. She has stopped going to the gym, stopped calling her mother, stopped laughing at her husband's jokes. She says she feels "dirty," like the assault is a stain that will never wash out. She avoids crowds, loud noises, and physical touch. She has not been intimate with her husband in six months. She says she is afraid to close her eyes at night because she sees his face.

She is a soldier who survived an assault. Now, she is fighting a war inside her own head.
